messages.author: f885e974e72cf61d
messages.subject: Shape departure from Brownian motion
parts:
Hi geomorph community, 

I'm investigating brain shape variation in mustelids which are thought to be an adaptive radiation. The phylogenetic signal for brain shape indicates a departure from Brownian motion (K=0.48039; p=1e-04). 

I've also run PGLS analyses with brain shape as a function of ecological/body size variables. I checked the phylogenetic signal of the residuals, and in nearly every case, K is between 0.5 to 0.6 and  p=1e-04. 

A suggested fix was to transform the phylogenetic tree before running further evolutionary analyses. My questions are: 
(1) What does it mean to "transform" a tree?
(2) Do you have any advice/resources on how to accomplish this? 
(3) Will this approach work with the new updates to Geomorph? Is there a different way to address this issue?

---------------------------------------
Unrelated side question: I keep getting different numbers for the PC loadings when I run a PCA, even though I'm using the exact same data set every time. It started happening after the big updates went through. Anyone know why this is? (e.g., one time the variance explained by PC1 may be 35%, and the next time running the analysis, it's 38%)

messages.author: fbfd20ce829c6c6c
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Shape departure from Brownian motion
parts:
Hi there, 

Phylogenetic transformations are different transformations of the matrix representations of the phylogeny. Some examples include the lambda transform, kappa, delta, etc. Some details are provided here (https://rdrr.io/rforge/motmot/man/transformPhylo.html), but I encourage you to track down the original papers for a full description of the different methods and what they mean.

Geomorph can do a lambda transform which I think might be what you are looking for. Take a look at the procD.pgls documentation here (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/geomorph/geomorph.pdf). The vignettes also go over how to optimize the parameter in regression using permutations. 

To answer your side question, I think folks might need more info (like the version numbers you are using).

Best,
Bryan

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Shape departure from Brownian motion
parts:
Bryan is correct that the tree scaling parameter, lambda, can be adjusted in procD.pgls.  There is an indirect way to also vary other scaling parameters, with the scaleCov function in RRPP.  This would require understanding how there parameters change a covariance matrix obtained from a tree, and working with the covariance matrix, directly, rather than the tree.  (The procD.pgls function calculates the covariance matrix from the tree, but covariance matrices could be obtained independently, e.g., with ape::vcv.phylo.)

Regarding this question:

Unrelated side question: I keep getting different numbers for the PC loadings when I run a PCA, even though I'm using the exact same data set every time. It started happening after the big updates went through. Anyone know why this is? (e.g., one time the variance explained by PC1 may be 35%, and the next time running the analysis, it's 38%)

You might not be using the exact same data, if obtained from gpagen (and I doubt the RRPP::ordinate or geomorph::gm.prcomp functions have changed in any way to induce drastically different loadings).  Several versions back (maybe the “big updates”), we started using faster algorithms for gpagen with sliding semilandmarks.  This meant more iterations could be run in the same amount of time, so we changed the default for max.iter from a maximum of 5 to 10 iterations (but one could run many more by changing the argument).  If you have semilandmarks and used the default arguments for gpagen, then what you might think are the exact same data are actually different data, if obtained before and after the update.

As a note on this and maybe as a surprise for some, GPA does not produce exact data.  The result depends on the convergence criterion used for this iterative procedure, if one requires convergence, or if not, when to stop the analysis.  These decisions are arbitrary.  Unless users wish to be confronted with an analysis that never ends, the default is to arrest the analysis after 10 iterations.  This is neither a rule of thumb nor a recommendation — we simply need to have something as a default.  With sliding landmarks, there is rarely convergence.  In fact, in some cases one could start to find results that are increasingly bad, as landmarks slide past each other, and variance among configurations is minimized by finding morphological impossibilities.  This is under-appreciated area of research in need of more theoretical development!  However, one could empirically explore for an optimal number of iterations (minimize variance while retaining morphological reasonableness).  

If you wish to have exactly the same data, first decide how many GPA iterations are needed, and always use that number for the set of raw landmarks.  If you want to try to make your results look like they used to, try max.iter = 5 and see if that helps.

Best,
Mike

Hi Bryan and Mike,

I am way delayed on this, but thank you very much for your responses and taking the time to help/explain!!

I had a quick follow up question, particularly in light of the new physignal.z function. I want to run multiple PGLS analyses to analyze the evolutionary relationship between shape and a bunch of other behavioral/ecological variables. Am I correct to assume that I will need to calculate lambda using the physignal.z function for each separate pgls regression that I run?

Again, huge thank you to you; I'm incredibly grateful for this community and your advice.
-Ani
